children.text:
The bar for Turing-complete is very low. The halting problem is to programming as Godel's incompleteness theorem is to metamathematics. Yet no one is seriously suggesting that we downgrade to axiomatic systems incapable of expressing Peano arithmetic, nor that our current axiomatic systems are impractical for proving theorems.

We cannot automatically and completely verify nontrivial semantic properties of arbitrary programs written in a Turing-complete language (Rice's theorem), but as long as we as humans can intuit correctness arguments for our programs, then formal methods will apply to it. Of course, declarative rather than imperative programming semantics tend to result in simpler correctness arguments, sidestepping reliance on global state and convoluted loop invariants.

children.text: Formal verification is not magic. It can execute deductive proofs, but the relevance and utility of those results is a question of human values. Spec bugs are a thing. Bad design is a thing. Out-of-scope usage is a thing. Even a halting oracle won't help with those.

> I recognize that there is probably no objective way to deductively prove it because of the Halting Problem etc.

There is. But it will only be reliable if every transitive dependency of your codebase, all the way down to the hardware level, has been formally verified. Failing that, you have to rely on opaque contracts at the boundaries, and those are just promises that may be mistaken.

The Halting problem, Rice's theorem, etc. only apply if your goal is to automatically and completely deduce properties or their violations for arbitrary programs. If your goal is simply to prove security and correctness properties for well-understood classes of programs in industry, then there are no fundamental obstructions.

The PHP2Shell vulnerability ended up being paradoxically comforting for me.

They turned frontier models loose on PHP, and the big one they found was based on a previously known logic flaw that was extremely difficult to exploit. Which makes sense: hence the need for frontier models.

And in the wild, while there have been many attempts and a few simple demo successes, the practical impact has seemed to be small, seemingly constrained by the length of the chain and the diversity of PHP configs.

In short, it was indeed a major vulnerability, but not magic (in the Arthur C Clarke sense).

I think ultimately the fear comes down to: do you believe that code can be secured. I recognize that there is probably no objective way to deductively prove it because of the Halting Problem etc. But if one believes code can be constructed to operate to spec, then there must be a limit to the damage an LLM can do, even a very smart one.

I think we are going through a phase where a lot of known triaged code shortcomings will get exposed and hopefully fixed. Sucks while it is happening. But not actually the first round of this type of evolution. And ultimately I think as before, we will come out the other side with more secure and durable technology.

children.author: varenc

> The broad issue is that you can turn DeepSeek-v6-unhinged loose on an arbitrary IP and exploit ~everything that is not developed and actively maintained by a billion-dollar company

Agreed. My fairly obscure company got hit by something like this last weekend. What stood out was the speed: attackers found something small, used it to uncover something else, and pivoted to clever exploits for the new thing within minutes. It hit a dozen of our apps in parallel within the span of a day, from a rotating pool of residential proxies, Tor, GCP and Cloudflare IPs.

I'm fairly confident it was LLM-driven. The payloads and throwaway accounts had names like "PT59553 TEST IGNORE" and "PocCorp1659r2", and it adapted to error messages the way a person reading them would, just never sleeping. A non-tech company with 100x the surface area and much more valuable data could be in big trouble.

Of course I used LLMs for the defense too, and they were amazing at log forensics and fixes. The annoying part was when I asked Opus 5.5 for clear repro cases of exactly what the attackers did, I hit the cyber safeguards. Opus was trying to keep the exploits for my own bespoke applications away from me. It was happy to fix things of course, but I worry if it really can't 'think' about actual exploits, its fixes will be less informed.

children.text:
> tangentially related data source

The used curl project as source which’s received mythos reports directly. What’s “tangential” about it?

The blog is misleading because it tries to characterize Project Glasswing's effectiveness through use of a tangentially related data source. A Project Glasswing vulnerability discovery most often occurs when a Glasswing partner points a Mythos-class model at its own, often proprietary, software. The data source (aka "ledger") is only for the Anthropic coordinated vulnerability disclosure program for open source software: in other words, Anthropic itself pointing a Mythos-class model at an OSS package, and then notifying the maintainer afterward that it had done this, and had findings to share. This OSS work is certainly useful, but the number of fixes reflects - in part - limited time availability by volunteer OSS maintainers, and Anthropic sometimes working without knowledge of the OSS project's threat model (the threat model is explicitly requested in the newer oss-scanner effort). Percentage fixed is often much higher for use of Glasswing with proprietary software, e.g., https://blog.cloudflare.com/cyber-frontier-models/ "Our research with Mythos Preview was conducted in a controlled environment against our own code; every vulnerability surfaced through this work was triaged, validated, and remediated where action was needed under Cloudflare's formal vulnerability management process."

> One reason why my experience could be an outlier is the effort I’ve gone to defining what the security properties of Fil-C are, to the point that there’s a crystal clear falsifiable boundary.

Building software boils down to defining things correctly. So, it sounds like you did most of the work here. Imagine that you took your definition and moved it into a formal specification (programming language) and then ran that to verify the security properties of your system. What's different?

Or, imagine that you took your original code as your specification language and then iterated on your understanding of it until it was correct. What's different?

Attention highlights and resolves bugs, so that's the baseline. In order for AI to get value, it has to be some kind of multiplier on your attention, but the reality is generally the opposite.

It’s true that I’m an AI adopter. My psychosis is pretty advanced. I’m running four clankers in parallel right now.

One reason why my experience could be an outlier is the effort I’ve gone to defining what the security properties of Fil-C are, to the point that there’s a crystal clear falsifiable boundary. So the bugs aren’t a matter of opinion or judgement. That helps clankers and it helps me when screening the bugs.

> concretely nothing of any significance has happened

This is a good point, but “cyber apocalypse dooming is an exaggeration” is a different statement than “bugs found by Anthropic aren’t real”. I agree that the dooming is an exaggeration. I don’t agree that Anthropic’s bugs suck.

Two reasons why bugs-found-by AI-are-really-scary and nothing-is-happening can be true at the same time:

1. Anthropic is sharing the bugs found by their most capable model with defenders, not attackers. Defenders are working overtime fixing those bugs before the embargo runs out.
